title: How to Make Up After a Fight With Your Partner — cv.cm
description: How to make up after a fight: calm down first, make a repair attempt, start softly and find the real need. Phrases that help or hurt, and when to get help.
h1: How do you make up after a fight with your partner?
answer: Calm down first: take a break of at least 20 minutes and say when you will come back. Then make a small repair attempt, start the talk gently with an "I" statement, and listen until you can summarize your partner's view. Find the need under the fight, agree on one next step, and apologize for your part.

sections.h: Why making up starts with calming down
body: Every couple fights. Whether it is called 吵架 in Chinese or 喧嘩 in Japanese, the goal after a fight (和好, 仲直り) is the same: feel like a team again and solve the problem a little better than before.

The first step is not talking. It is calming down. The Gottman Institute describes "flooding": in a heated argument the body goes into a stress state, the heart beats fast, and it becomes hard to listen or think clearly. People who are flooded often shut down or say things they regret. Their advice is to pause and take about 20 minutes alone doing something soothing, such as walking or reading, before going back to the talk.
A break is different from the silent treatment. A healthy break has a reason and a return time. Punishing silence has neither. Say something like:

ul: "I'm too upset to talk well right now. I need 30 minutes. I'll come back and we'll finish this."
"I want to sort this out with you. Can we talk again after dinner?"

body: During the break, try not to replay the fight or plan your next argument. Breathe slowly, go outside, or do something with your hands. Then come back when you said you would. See cv.cm's article on the silent treatment for more on the difference.

sections.h: Repair attempts: small moves that stop a fight from getting worse
body: The Gottman Institute calls a repair attempt any word or action, even a silly one, that stops negativity from growing. Strong couples are not couples who never fight. They are couples who repair early and often, and who accept each other's repair attempts.

ul: "Can we start over? I said that badly."
"I'm sorry, that came out harsher than I meant."
"I know we both care about this. Let's slow down."
A hand on the arm, a hug, a shared joke, or making them a cup of tea.
In a chat app, a sticker or message like "I don't want to fight with you. Can we talk tonight?"

body: If your partner makes a repair attempt, try to accept it, even if you are still a little upset. Pushing it away ("Don't try to be funny now") usually makes the fight last longer.

Gottman's research found that the first few minutes of a conflict talk often predict how it ends. A harsh start (blame, sarcasm, "you always") usually leads to a bad talk. A "soft start-up" describes the problem and your feelings without attacking your partner's character.
A simple formula: "I feel (emotion) about (specific situation), and I need (positive request)."

head: Instead of
Try
rows: "I felt hurt when you looked at your phone while I was talking. I need you to put it down when we talk about something important."
"I felt left out when you made plans for the weekend without asking me. Can we decide together next time?"
"I get stressed when we're late to my parents' place. Could we leave 15 minutes earlier on Sunday?"
"I'm still upset, but I want to understand you. Can you tell me what was going on for you?"

body: Talk about one issue at a time. Bringing up every old problem in one talk makes it impossible to solve anything.

sections.h: Listen, summarize and find the real need
body: Most fights are not really about the dishes or the late reply. Underneath there is a need: to feel respected, to feel important, to feel safe, to have some freedom, or to share the work fairly. Making up works when both people feel heard about that need.

ol: Let one person speak first. The other only listens, without defending.
The listener summarizes: "So you felt alone when I went out with my friends right after your bad day. Is that right?"
The speaker corrects anything that was missed.
Ask about the need: "What would have helped you feel better in that moment?"
Each person names one thing that was their part: "My part was that I snapped at you instead of saying I was tired."
Agree on one small next step, not a perfect solution: "Next time one of us has a bad day, we'll say it, and the other will check in before making plans."

body: Summarizing is not agreeing. You can understand your partner's view and still see things differently. Many couple problems never fully go away; the goal is to talk about them without hurting each other.
If you need to apologize, cv.cm's article on how to apologize to your partner explains the parts of a real apology.

sections.h: Phrases that help and phrases that hurt

head: Type
Helps
Hurts
rows: Walking out without a word, or not replying for days
"You made me..." or "You're crazy for feeling that"
"I said sorry, what more do you want?"
"Tell me more. I want to understand."
Eye-rolling, laughing at them, or checking your phone
"What can we do differently next time?"
"You'll never change" or threats to break up
"I'm glad we talked. I love you."

body: Gottman calls contempt (mocking, insults, eye-rolling) the most damaging pattern in conflict. If you notice it in yourself, stop and repair right away.

sections.h: When the same fight keeps coming back
body: If you have the same argument every week, it is usually a sign that the deeper need has not been named, or that one of you does not believe the other will change. Some steps:

ul: Write down what the fight is really about for each of you, in one sentence.
Pick a calm time, not right after a fight, to talk about the pattern itself: "We keep fighting about chores. What do you think is really going on?"
Make one concrete agreement and check on it in two weeks.
Learn each other's conflict style. cv.cm's conflict style test shows whether you tend to compete, avoid, accommodate, compromise or collaborate.
If you feel stuck after many tries, couples counselling can help you both feel heard with a neutral person in the room.

sections.h: When a fight is not normal
body: Disagreements are normal. Fear is not. A fight is a sign of a deeper problem, or of abuse, when:

ul: You are afraid of your partner's anger or change what you say to avoid it.
Your partner threatens you, breaks things, blocks the door, or hurts you.
They threaten to leave, hurt themselves or hurt you to win arguments.
They punish you with days of silence, or control your money, phone or friends.
You are always the one who must apologize, whatever happened.

body: If this is happening, it is not your fault, and better communication alone will not fix it. Couples counselling is often not advised when one partner is abusive; individual support is safer.

body.note: If you are in danger, contact local emergency services. You can also talk to a domestic violence helpline. In the US, examples are thehotline.org and, for young people, loveisrespect.org; or contact a local service where you live.

faq.q: Who should apologize first after a fight?
faq.a: The person who is calm first. Apologizing for your part does not mean you accept all the blame. It often makes it easier for your partner to own their part too.

faq.q: How long should you wait to talk after a fight?
faq.a: At least 20 minutes, so the body can calm down. Many couples do best talking again the same day, or within a day. Always say when you will come back to it.

faq.q: Is it okay to go to bed angry?
faq.a: Yes, sometimes. A tired, late-night talk can make things worse. Say "I love you, let's talk about this tomorrow morning", and then do it.

faq.q: How do you make up with your partner over text?
faq.a: Send a short repair message such as "I'm sorry for how I spoke earlier. I want to talk properly. Can we call tonight?" Save the real conversation for a call or in person.

faq.q: Is fighting in a relationship healthy?
faq.a: Disagreeing is normal and can help couples understand each other. What matters is how you fight: without contempt or fear, and with repair afterwards.
